transcript:
[00:00] Avery Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, quick roll call — Avery from Redwood, Priya from the SE team.
[00:08] Carlos Mendes: Carlos here, Elena and Tom on as well. Morning.
[00:12] Avery Chen: Great. Real quick agenda — selection confirmation, pinning strategy, and soft escape hatches. We'll leave ten for next steps.
[00:22] Priya Rao: Yep — and I'll talk through the fallback routing patterns we prototyped.
[00:30] Tom Bishop: Sounds good, we got the pilot results you sent yesterday, skimmed them. A few Qs.
[00:36] Avery Chen: Perfect, Carlos, want to start with your take on which model your team prefers from the catalog?
[00:44] Carlos Mendes: Right, so we ran the baseline on two candidate flavors — a 13B optimized quantized variant and the 30B fp16 baseline. The 13B hits our latency SLO in most cases, like median is ~110 ms, p95 around 420ms on our tests. The 30B gives better quality on long contexts but p95 climbs to 1.2s which is rough for the chat flow.
[01:10] Elena Park: And cost delta was about 2.7x between the 30B and 13B, correct? Some of the burst hours would double cost.
[01:18] Priya Rao: That's inline with what we saw. For a production SLO at 300ms p95, 13B quantized or an intermediate 20B quantized profile is usually the sweet spot. But also you can use soft fallbacks to route non-critical requests to a cheaper model.
[01:34] Carlos Mendes: We like the idea of soft fallbacks but we worry about semantic drift — the cheaper model sometimes hallucinated in our test prompts.
[01:42] Avery Chen: Totally reasonable. Our recommendation is to pin primary to the 13B-quant profile for chat and use a slightly different pinned variant for generation-heavy endpoints. Then set up a routing policy: normal route -> primary; when latency breaches or queue depth rises, route to fallback model but with a QA gate for certain prompt types.
[02:00] Tom Bishop: QA gate meaning what, like a classifier or simple heuristic?
[02:04] Priya Rao: Could be both — we commonly use a small classifier to flag risky prompts (PII, system instructions) and force them to the primary model. For low-risk conversational turns we allow the lightweight fallback. Also, you can shadow requests to the fallback to monitor drift without exposing outputs.
[02:23] Carlos Mendes: Shadowing helps. Can we get an example of the routing config?
[02:27] Priya Rao: Yes — I'll share a snippet. It contains routing priorities, thresholds for avg latency and queue length, and an escape-hatch that reverts to primary if semantic divergence exceeds X% across a sliding window.
[02:40] Avery Chen: Note — the divergence metric is often noisy, so set it conservatively. We also recommend time-based canaries for version switches.
[02:48] Elena Park: On the private networking side, we need the exact outbound IPs and TLS finger prints for firewall whitelisting. Also audit log retention policies.
[02:58] Avery Chen: We'll include the IP list and security docs. Redwood Private supports KMS integration for keying and we can route logs to your SIEM.
[03:06] Carlos Mendes: Awesome. A question on model pin rollbacks — what's the safe rollback runway? If we pin a model and see quality regressions, how fast can we revert?
[03:16] Priya Rao: The runtime supports version-gated rollbacks — you can revert configally within minutes but practical rollback also depends on cache warming. If you rollback to a previous model without warm KV cache, you may see a brief latency spike. So we recommend a rollback strategy that includes a short ramp (25% -> 50% -> 100%) and monitor the key metrics.
[03:36] Tom Bishop: Hmm, cache warming concern is big for us. Any tricks for minimizing the penalty?
[03:40] Priya Rao: A couple: preload common prefixes via synthetic traffic, keep a shadow pool warm for the fallback model, or use warm-start routing for a subset of endpoints. Also lower the batch size temporarily to reduce variability.
[03:54] Carlos Mendes: Can Redwood do the synthetic preload as part of the pilot?
[03:58] Avery Chen: We can run a small warmup job as part of the canary window, yes. We'll coordinate with Elena for allowed endpoints and traffic shaping.
[04:06] Elena Park: We'll need the privacy note for synthetic data.
[04:09] Avery Chen: We'll redact or use no-PHI patterns; we'll send the playbook.
[04:14] Priya Rao: Back to catalog — we suggested three candidate pinned versions in the doc: Rwin-13Q-v2, Redwood-20Q-beta, and Rwin-30-fp. Your team said Rwin-13Q-v2 looks best for baseline.
[04:28] Carlos Mendes: Yes. But for weekend batch summaries we might route to the 30B ephemeral.
[04:34] Tom Bishop: For the summary use-case, latency isn't critical, so 30B is ideal.
[04:38] Avery Chen: Great, so plan is: primary pin = Rwin-13Q-v2 for chat; heavy-generation endpoints pinned to 30B with scheduled windows; fallback model = 13B cheap variant with stricter QA gating.
[04:54] Carlos Mendes: On metrics, what should we watch?
[04:57] Priya Rao: p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, cost per 1k tokens, semantic divergence (via embedding similarity), and failure/error rate. We'll provide the monitoring dashboard template.
[05:08] Tom Bishop: About costs — can you show per-token cost assuming our 30-day traffic profile? We sent last month's usage.
[05:16] Avery Chen: We'll run that calc and return a sheet with cost/latency tradeoffs across pins and quantization levels. Expect that by Friday.
[05:23] Carlos Mendes: Good. One more thing — edge-case safety. We saw hallucinations on prompts that begin with system-like instructions. How do we lock that down?
[05:33] Priya Rao: Two approaches: input sanitization and pre-classification. Add a strict content filter that demotes or blocks system instruction-like tokens; second, route to primary for anything flagged. Also, use structured outputs or function calling to constrain responses.
[05:48] Elena Park: For compliance we need audit trails of routing decisions. Is that available?
[05:52] Avery Chen: Yes — routing decisions and model version chosen are logged per-request and can be exported to your SIEM.
[05:59] Carlos Mendes: Ok, let's talk canary timing and rollback windows. We prefer a weekend low-traffic window, next Tuesday is risky. How about Mar 30th 00:00–02:00 UTC?
[06:10] Avery Chen: Mar 30th works for our ops team. We'll propose a rollout plan: 10% -> 40% -> 100% over 30 minutes with 10-minute holds, and immediate rollback trigger conditions.
[06:24] Tom Bishop: For rollback triggers, recommend alert thresholds: >10% semantic divergence, >20% increase in p95, or >1% error rate spike.
[06:33] Priya Rao: Agree. We'll codify those thresholds in the playbook.
[06:38] Carlos Mendes: Sounds fair. Anything else on model selection?
[06:42] Elena Park: Just to confirm, we'll have the fallback routing implemented with shadowing for at least 48h before turning it live.
[06:49] Priya Rao: Yes, shadow for 48h and evaluate drift metrics.
[06:53] Avery Chen: Alright, quick recap — Redwood to share detailed cost/latency sheet and model catalog link; Priya to share routing config and fallback playbook snippet; BrightRoute to run evals and confirm network constraints; schedule canary for 2026-03-30.
[07:12] Tom Bishop: Thanks all.
[07:14] Carlos Mendes: Thanks — we'll start the evals and share results.
[07:17] Elena Park: We'll check firewall rules and get back.
[07:19] Avery Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with notes and the artifacts.
[07:22] [end of recorded portion]
